key_insight: The 2026 public charge rule is projected to reduce NYC immigrants’ primary care use and increase premature mortality, with larger harms under more severe avoidance of coverage and care.
clinical_relevance: For health systems and policymakers, the findings suggest that policy-driven chilling effects on coverage can translate into measurable downstream losses in preventive care and survival among immigrant communities.
method: Deterministic compartmental simulation using ordinary differential equations (ODEs).
Calibrated with 2023 NYC vital statistics and American Community Survey data.
Scenario analysis modeled conservative, moderate, and aggressive avoidance/disenrollment effects using prior estimates linking coverage access to health outcomes.
evidence_signal: Projected estimates showed 4.1% to 9.9% lower primary care access, 5.1% to 12.2% fewer doctor visits, and 4.4% to 10.6% higher premature mortality at 5 years, with larger mortality increases by 20 years.
watch_item: This is a model-based projection that depends on prior effect estimates and assumptions about chilling-effect behavior, so real-world impacts may differ.
paper_title: The 2026 public charge rule and long-term health impacts among NYC immigrants: a simulation study
